texts: 126A. Black moves. The position on the c-file calls for a discovered attack on White’s Queen by a move of Black’s Bishop.
126B. White moves. Black has “discovered” an attack on White’s Queen; at the same time the unmasking Bishop creates the terrible threat ... xh2 mate. White must lose at least a piece (3 c4, xc4).
127A. White moves. He begins by driving the Black Rook at f8 into position for the discovered attack pattern: 1 e7. Black replies 1 ... e8. Now 2 b4 threatens 3 xe8 mate, or 3 xb4.

127B. Black moves. He cannot move his Queen in such a way as to guard the unprotected Rook. Hence he must give up his Queen to stave off the mate. A particularly virulent example of discovered attack!

title: QUIZ ON DISCOVERED ATTACKS
texts: 128. White moves. By what discovered attack does he win the Queen?
129. White moves. By what discovered attack does he win a piece?
130. Black moves. By what discovered attack does he win the Queen?
131. Black moves. By what discovered attack does he win a piece?

DISCOVERED CHECK is an intensified and hence even more potent form of discovered attack. Each stratagem confers the advantage of simultaneously blasting two enemy forces. The stepped-up power of the discovered check consists in this: one of the two vulnerable targets is the opponent’s King.
The discovered check keeps its victim busy; meanwhile, the unmasking piece is free to venture anywhere – to capture, to threaten to capture, or to pluck off pieces by the “hit-and-run” method.

title: BASIC PATTERN FOR DISCOVERED CHECK
texts: 132. White moves. He will give the discovered check on the e-file. In the diagram, Black’s King is screened from check by the White Knight. Any move of the Knight will keep Black’s King busy getting out of check from the unmasked White Rook.

Meanwhile the Knight will be free to capture, or threaten to capture, any important object in his range. As the most effective continuation, White chooses 1 c5+ attacking Black’s Queen with the Knight while he opens fire on Black’s King with the Rook. You will observe that Black has no time to save his Queen! Priority of check leaves Black no choice.

133A. White moves. His seventh rank forms the basic pattern for a discovered check: any move by the Bishop will discover a check by White’s Rook. The problem is to find a target for the white-squared Bishop. This is done by forcing the Knight to a white square: 1 b4!

133B. Black moves. His Knight is lost! 1 ... b7? or 1 ... b3? is out of the question. 1 ... c4 is answered by 2 xc4+ leaving Black no time to capture (remember the priority of check!). So Black tries 1 ... c6, but 2 d5+ wins the piece.

134A. White moves. He begins with a startling sacrifice: 1 f7! forks Black’s Queen and Rook. After 1 ... xf7 the f-file forms the pattern for a discovered check: 2 fxg5+. Now we see the point of the diabolical first move.

134B. Black moves. His King has been lured into occupying the same file as White’s Rook. The f-Pawn opens the way for the Rook’s gunfire and stabs at the Black Queen. However Black may play, his Queen is lost.

135A. Black moves. Any Rook move by Black will subject his opponent to check while the Rook tries to gobble up material. The most forceful way is 1 ... xa2+; 2 g1, g2+; but after 3 h1, what has White gained?!

135B. Black moves. He has altered the position slightly but decisively. The pattern for discovered check remains, but in a more deadly form: White’s Bishop is no longer supported by a Pawn! Now comes 3 ... b2+; 4 g1, xb3.

136A. Black moves. By removing the extraneous factors in complicated positions, you produce the design for winning; thus the “brilliant” 1 ... xg3! forces 2 fxg3. What has Black achieved by the sacrifice? How will he turn it to account? By means of a discovered check.

136B. Black moves. By sacrificing his Queen, he forced the opening of the diagonal between Black’s Bishop and White’s King, creating the basic pattern for a discovered check. White’s Queen is the biggest prey in sight, so Black pounces on it with 2 ... d1+.
137A. White moves. He plays 1 d7+ (double attack), when 1 ... c7 is compulsory. Now 2 xc7+, xc7 and we have the basic pattern for discovered check on the c-file. So: 3 f8+!

137B. Black moves. His Bishop is attacked, but cannot be saved. The Black King has been put in check by White’s double-duty Bishop. Once the King moves out of check, White plays 4 xg7, winning easily.
138A. White moves. His first move is a simple method of forcing a position which he has already pictured in his mind. The image derives from the basic pattern for discovered check:

138B. Black moves. His King and Queen are attacked. The King must get out of check (priority!); hence the Queen is lost. White brought about this result by creating the basic pattern for discovered check on the diagonal from his Bishop to Black’s King. White knew what he was looking for.

title: QUIZ ON DISCOVERED CHECK
texts: 139. White moves. How does he win the Queen by a discovered check?
140. White moves. How does he win the Queen by a discovered check?
141. Black moves. How does he win a piece by discovered check?

JUST AS discovered check is an intensified form of the discovered attack, so double check is an even more crushing form of discovered check. The latter is brought about by a piece which unmasks a check. In double check, the unmasking piece also gives check. Thus, capture or interposition is ruled out as a defense: the harassed King must fend for himself. Double checks are rare, but when they occur, they must be exploited to the limit. They often force checkmate directly or else score heavy gains of material.

title: BASIC PATTERN FOR DOUBLE CHECK
texts: 142. Black moves. He ignores the fact that his Queen is en prise, for he notes that his Queen is in line with the hostile King, separated only by a piece which can also give check. This is the basic pattern for double check. Black plays 1 ... f3+, giving checkmate on the move. White cannot capture, he cannot interpose, he cannot move his King.

143A. White moves. He begins by examining possible captures and checks. 1 xg6 leads to nothing, so he turns to 1 g5+, noting that Black can reply 1 ... xf7. Can reply?! – no: must reply! This excites White’s interest, for he sees that he can force Black into a double check. The play goes: 1 g5+!, xf7; and now we have the pattern for a double check.

144A. Black moves. The mighty Bishop on the “long diagonal” leading to White’s King is the star actor here. But the diagonal is momentarily blocked by a White Pawn. To suggest the obstacle is to remove it: 1 ... xf3! Black surrenders his Queen in order to achieve the basic pattern for a double check. There follows 2 xe2, xf1 mate!

145A. White moves. The position of his Rook on the g-file gives him an idea for constructing the basic pattern for a double check. The g-file is now half open; do you see how it can be forced open all the way against Black’s vulnerable King? The answer: 1 xh5!, gxh5; 2 xe6+.

143B. White moves. He completes the combination with 2 d6 mate! This drastic finish bears out the deadly reputation of the double check: the Knight cannot be captured because of the Queen check, and interposition is impossible because of the Knight check! All that remains is self-help: move the King. But all exits are blocked. The King is checkmated.

144B. Again the double check has done its deadly work. White cannot capture the Bishop or interpose to its attack, because the Rook is giving check. Similarly, the Rook’s attack cannot be parried because of the Bishop check!
(Note, by the way, that after 1 ... xf3! the reply 2 xb7 is answered by 2 ... xc4, leaving White hopelessly behind in material.)
145B. Black moves. His King is doubly checked, and must move. The impudent Knight is therefore immune. After Black’s King moves, there follows 3 xc7 and White has won a piece.
An important feature of this combination is the unprotected state of Black’s Queen. Loose pieces are the landmarks of combinations.

title: QUIZ ON DOUBLE CHECK
texts: 146. Black moves. If he plays 1 ... xg4, how does White win at once?
147. Black moves. He has just sacrificed his Queen. How does he mate in two moves?

THE VIEW THAT “no man can serve two masters” is often forcibly demonstrated on the chessboard. When a piece has two duties – protecting two other pieces, or protecting a piece and also guarding an important square from invasion – that piece may be overworked. In such situations, everything appears well defended; yet they collapse when pressure is applied to the weak point. Even tightlyknit positions, which are invulnerable to pins, Knight forks, double attacks and the like, are prone to topple on the first thrust at an overworked piece.

title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE
texts: 148. Black moves. His Queen attacks a Rook, his Knight attacks the Bishop. The Knight at d2 serves no defensive purpose, being pinned and therefore paralyzed. Hence White’s Queen must guard the menaced pieces. To prove that the Queen is overworked, Black plays 1 ... xf3+. After 2 xf3 White’s Queen no longer guards the Rook, so that 2 ... xb1+ wins.

149A. White moves. Searching for a weakness in Black’s position, he spots it in Black’s e-Pawn. This Pawn guards the Knight at d6 (which is attacked by a White Bishop) and also the Bishop at f6 (which is attacked by a White Rook). Thus the e-Pawn has a double task; it is overworked; it can be undermined. The most logical course is 1 xd6 forcing 1 ... exd6.

150A. White moves. Black’s pieces seem amply protected, but the fact that they are mutually dependent on each other for support is thoughtprovoking. The overworked motif may be present! Sure enough, the Rook at h8 guards both Rook and Bishop, which are both attacked by the Rook at g7. The Rook at h8 is therefore overworked. There follows 1 xh7!

151A. Black moves. He wants to play ... e2, threatening ... xh2 mate or ... g2 mate. At first sight ... e2 seems impossible, as the square in question is guarded by White’s Rook at e1. But this Rook also has to guard the Rook at f1, and is therefore an overworked piece! We undermine it with 1 ... e2!

149B. White moves. The overworked e-Pawn has now been displaced, no longer defending the Bishop. So White continues 2 xf6, with a piece to the good. (Sometimes there is more than one way of undermining a piece. For example, White could have played 1 xf6, exf6; 2 xd6 with two pieces for a Rook. But 1 xd6 is even stronger.)
150B. Black moves. He cannot regain the lost piece! Whichever Rook is captured, his other Rook goes lost. Thus if 1 ... xg1; 2 xh8 or 1 ... xh7; 2 xg8.
This combination is hard to see, for 1 xh7! leaves White’s Rooks disunited and unprotected. Searching for every possible capture is particularly important against overworked pieces.

151B. White moves. He is menaced by two different mates on the second rank, and the only plausible defense 2 xe2 allows 2 ... xf1 mate in reply. In Diagram 151B, White’s Rook at e1 is an overworked piece; it cannot defend against every threat. The brilliant 1 ... e2! is easy to see once we realize that the overworked piece must be undermined.

152A. White moves. There are Knight forks in the air! Following the maxim that one must look at every check and capture, White studies 1 xb7 forking Queen and Rook. Then he notices 1 xe6+ forking King and Queen. But in each case, the fork is guarded by Black’s Bishop. In each case?! That is our clue! We play 1 xb7!

153A. White moves. His first impulse is to move away his Queen from attack. But note this: the Bishop which is doing the attacking is guarded by Black’s Queen. But the other Black Bishop at e7 is also protected by the Queen from capture by White’s Rook. Doesn’t that make Black’s Queen an overworked piece? And if so, shouldn’t White do something about it, instead of meekly retreating? He plays 1 xe7!

154A. Black moves. He sees that White’s pinned Knight is protected by King and Queen – two pieces – and attacked by two pieces. He also sees that White’s Bishop is protected by the Queen. In other words, the protection of the Queen is common to both the Knight and Bishop. To undermine the overworked Queen, Black plays 1 ... xd2+. White re plies 2 xd2.

152B. Black moves. He sees now that his Bishop is an overworked piece. To get rid of the Knight fork, he plays 1 ... xb7 (1 ... c7; 2 xd8 is hopeless for him). Now comes 2 xe6+, a family check which attacks King, Queen and Rook. Black’s game collapses.
The poor Bishop could not be in two places at once!
153B. Black moves. His attack on the Queen has become meaningless, as 1 ... xf3 is answered by 2 xd7, and White has gained a piece.
Therefore Black tries 1 ... xe7 (as good as any); White continues with 2 xd5+ winning two pieces for a Rook and thus remaining with a decisive material advantage.
Again we see the value of looking at every capture and check.
154B. Black moves. White’s Queen has been diverted from the protection of the Bishop, so that Black can now wind up with the killing 2 ... xf3+, forking King and Queen.
(Coming back to 154A, we note that Black can also win with 1 ... xf3+; 2 xf3, xd2+ etc. The overworked piece can frequently be undermined in more than one way.)

155A. White moves. Black’s game looks solid, but it has weaknesses. The weak chink in his armor is the Bishop at f6, which has to be guarded by Black’s Queen; Black’s g-Pawn, being pinned, has no defensive value. But Black’s Queen also has to guard the Bishop at b7, so our problem boils down to this: how can we harry the Queen? Answer: 1 e4!

156A. White moves. Once we spot the overworked piece, the method of undermining it is as delightful as it is logical. In this case it is the Black Rook at f8 which is overworked, improbable as it may seem. This Rook has the duty of guarding the Queen and the other Rook at h8. The undermining process begins with 1 d8+!

157A. White moves. Is Black’s Queen overworked? The Queen protects the Rook and also prevents mate at Black’s g7. Yet the Queen is not overworked, as after 1 xg5, xg5 the mate is still guarded. To convert the Queen into an overworked piece, it is necessary to shift the scene of the exchange of Rooks. This is done by 1 h4+.

155B. Black moves. If he plays 1 ... xe4, then 2 xf6+ forks King and Queen. Hence Black tries 1 ... c7 but loses a piece after 2 xb7, xb7; 3 xf6+ etc. (The pinned state of the g-Pawn is crucial!) 1 e4! is an ideal example of undermining an overworked piece, as the Queen can no longer guard both Bishops. Maxim: Disturb the overworked piece!

156B. Black moves. He is in check, and he realizes that the checking move will draw the Rook away from f8, so that one of the guarded pieces will lose its protection. Thus if 1 ... xd8; 2 xf4 wins the Queen. Or if 1 ... c7; 2 xf4, xf4; 3 xh8 with an easy win. Rarely has an overworked piece been undermined so artistically.

157B. Black moves. He finds that the check is not easy to answer: if 1 ... g8; 2 e7+ forks King and Queen. He therefore interposes: 1 ... h5. But now the scene of the exchange has been shifted. The Queen must stand guard over two unrelated points and thus becomes an overworked piece. The proof: 2 xh5+, xh5; 3 xg7 mate.

158A. White moves. Black’s Rook at h8 is chained to his post to prevent xh7 mate. Consequently the Rook may become an overworked piece. If it is given another duty, it will crack under the strain! White plays 1 f8!, relying on the fact that 1 ... xf8? would permit 2 xh7 mate. Black’s best chance is to give up the exchange, but let us suppose he tries 1 ... e8.

159A. White moves. He sees that the Black Queen is overworked: it has the double duty of guarding the f-Pawn and the Rook at c6. A capture by White will undermine the overworked piece – but what is the right capture? 1 xc6?, xc6 brings the Rook at a7 to the defense of the f-Pawn. So we try reverse English: 1 xf7+!

160A. White moves. The play pivots on the fact that Black’s Queen is overworked: she defends the b-Pawn and also prevents f8 mate. White fastens on this weakness by playing 1 xb7! As 1 ... xb7? permits 2 f8 mate, Black has nothing better than 1 ... c7. Now his Rook at d8 guards the mate on the last rank.

158B. White moves. He sees that Black’s Rook at h8 must now protect its brother Rook at e8 in addition to preventing xh7 mate! Now the Black Rook is really overworked! White exploits the strained position of the Rook by 2 xe8 and if 2 ... xe8; 3 xh7 mate.
The instructive feature here is the way that Black’s Rook was forced to become overworked.
159B. Black moves. He must play 1 ... xf7 (if 1 ... h8??; 2 g8 mate). Now comes 2 xf7+, (or )xf7; 3 xc6. White’s combination has won the exchange and a Pawn.
This is a case where transposition of moves would spoil the whole winning process. Carelessness or lack of determination often mars such winning possibilities.

160B. White moves. True, the mate on the back rank is stopped, but White is merciless: he spots a newly created weakness in Black’s camp. Black’s Queen is still overworked, guarding the Knight at c7 and also parrying the threat of f6+, made possible by the removal of the Knight to c7. So: 2 xc7!, xc7; 3 f6+ forcing mate!

title: QUIZ ON THE OVERWORKED PIECE
texts: 161. Black moves. White’s Rook at c1 guards the other White Rook and the Bishop as well. What capture undermines the overworked piece?
162. Black moves. White’s Queen prevents mate at g2 and also guards the Knight at d3. What capture demonstrates that the White Queen is overworked?
163. White moves. Black’s Knight at c6 defends two pieces. How does White prove that this Knight is overworked?
164. Black’s Queen guards two pieces. How does White profit by this circumstance to win a piece at once?

NAPOLEON, who was a great general but only a mediocre chess player, coined the phrase “An army travels on its stomach” to emphasize the importance of supplying soldiers with food. Break the line of communications between soldiers and their food resources, and they are lost. On the chessboard we can think of the attacked piece as a soldier. When direct threats against it fail, we can aim our attack against its support. If we can destroy, drive off or exchange the guard of a piece, then we can win that piece.

title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD
texts: 165. White moves. Black’s King is tied down to the defense of his Queen. If the King can be forced away, the Queen will be lost. The most forceful move is always a check or a capture. White plays 1 g7+! forcing the removal of the piece guarding the Queen. Black must play 1 ... xg7, whereupon 2 xe7+ is decisive.

166A. White moves. He sees that the vulnerable point in Black’s game is the Rook on d5, guarded only by the Black Queen. With White’s Queen and both Black Rooks in line, thoughts of a double attack suggest themselves. The guard must be removed! Therefore: 1 e7! This forces Black to abandon the protection of the Rook, with the continuation 1 ... xe7; 2 xd5+.
167A. Black moves. A little combination wins for Black, though he is behind in material: 1 ... d1+; 2 e1, c5.
He attacks the Queen which protects the Rook. White replies 3 a5, since the Queen must remain on the diagonal leading to the Rook.

168A. White moves. He can play 1 e4, attacking the Queen with his Knight, and meanwhile discovering attack on the Knight at f7 with his own Queen. But this would be pointless, as the Knight is guarded by the Black Bishop. “Is guarded by ...” – there is our clue! Remove the guard!
166B. Black moves. The double attack costs him his Rook at a8.
White’s task in 166A was to visualize the position with the guard (Black’s Queen) removed from the board. This led him to 1 e7 as the most forcible way to achieve his goal.
In chess you do not wait for things to happen – you make them happen. If not, things will happen to you.
167B. Black moves. He strikes at the Queen once more by 3 ... b6, and wins the Queen (and eventually the game) as the Queen must leave the vital diagonal.
168B. White moves. Now that the Black Knight at f7 has no protection, 2 xf7 wins easily.

Where pieces protect pieces, the mortality rate is high! The protecting piece is subject to exchange, capture or eviction. As pointed out in 167B, Pawns are more sturdy defenders; uprooting them is an expensive process.

169A. White moves. He can simplify with 1 xe8+, xe8; 2 xc7, e2+; 3 h3 etc., which is good enough. But he looks for a quick win, based on removing the guard. The indications are there, for the Black Rook, which can be captured with check, is guarded only by the Queen. White plays 1 g4+!

170A. Black moves. His pin on the Knight would normally yield dividends by the application of more pressure – say by ... e6. But he has no time, as his own Bishop is attacked. But there is a quicker course. The unhappy Knight is protected only by pieces. Therefore Black removes one of the guards with 1 ... xg2+.

171A. White moves. He has an open file for his King’s Rook, and simple doubling on this file would suffice to win (1 h5, g6; 2 ah1 etc.). But there is a quicker, more dynamic way, based on the fact that Black’s defensive force is scattered: 1 h7+! The Rook must be captured (if 1 ... g8? or 1 ... g6?; 2 xf7 mate).

169B. Black moves. To save his Queen he must play 1 ... xg4. Now White does not continue 2 fxg4? (which leaves him a Rook down after 2 ... xe1). Instead he continues as planned: 2 xe8+, now that the Rook’s defender has been removed. Black has no time to save his Queen (priority of check!). After 2 ... g7; 3 fxg4 wins easily.

170B. White moves. His reply is forced: 2 xg2. Now that White’s Knight has lost a vital prop, Black has a winning double attack: 2 ... xe4+ (2 ... xe4+ is also good); 3 xe4, xe4+ followed by 4 ... xb1. An inventory of the final position shows Black to be a piece ahead, with an easy win. The winning method here is of great practical value.

171B. Black moves. As we have shown, 1 ... xh7 is forced. But now White has removed the only defender (the Black King!) of the f-Pawn, or, more exactly, of the square f7. After 2 xf7+, Black has 2 ... h8 or 2 ... h6; in either event 3 h1+ puts Black out of his misery. In this case, removing the guard led to a mating attack.

172A. White moves. He attacks the hostile Knight twice. It is defended twice. Both guards are pieces. If either defender can be captured or driven off, the Knight will be lost – his guard will be removed. These reflections lead logically to 1 b6, which forks both guards: the Rook and Bishop.

173A. Black moves. His Rook attacks White’s Knight, which is defended by a Bishop. Remove this guard and White’s position collapses. As in 172A, a Knight fork does the trick: 1 ... c4. The menaced Rook must stay on the second rank to guard the Bishop, hence 2 c2. Black is well on the way to achieving his objective.

174A. White moves. He sees that the position of the hostile Knight is shaky. It has two defenders – but both can be knocked out. How? Not by 1 xd6?, cxd6; 2 dxe5, dxe5 and the Knight is guarded by a sturdy Pawn. We need a more accurate order of moves: 1 dxe5!, xe5 (if 1 ... xe5; 2 xf4 wins a piece). Now to remove a guard.

172B. Black moves. He plays 1 ... b8. This is inadequate, but he has nothing better. Now there follows 2 xa8, xa8 and, amusingly enough, neither of the Black Knight’s guards is functioning. White now captures the Knight, with a piece ahead. Maxim: Knock out the prop, and the piece falls!

173B. Black moves. Has he really come nearer to his goal? He has blocked the action of his own Rook, and even permitted White to increase the Knight’s protection. But, as has been pointed out, pieces are unstable guards. Now comes 2 ... xb2; 3 xb2. Both defenders are gone; 3 ... xc3 wins the piece after all. An impressive example because of its simplicity.

174B. White moves. With the Knight guarded by two pieces, the rest is easy: remove one of the guards. The move we want is 2 xd6, and whichever way Black recaptures, we continue with 3 xf4. The way in which White proves that the Knight is inadequately defended is genuinely instructive.

175A. White moves. His attack is concentrated against the pinned Knight. He can remove the guard (the King) by 1 h8+, but after 1 ... xh8; 2 xg6 he has lost material: the Knight is less valuable than the sacrificed Rook. But try a different order of moves: 1 xg6+ xg6.

176A. White moves. Our familiarity with removing the guard suggests that Black’s Queen, being defended by only the Knight, is in difficulties. But we must force Black’s hand, else he escapes by ... xd2+. What we need is a forcing move which reduces Black’s choice of a reply; we look for a capture or a check. Therefore: 1 e7+.

177A. White moves. His Rook menaces Black’s Bishop, which is guarded by his Knight, which in turn is guarded by a Pawn. To remove the guard, it is necessary to “destroy the house that Jack built” by removing the Pawn that guards the Knight that guards the Bishop.

175B. White moves. He has forced a position where the pinned piece (the Queen) is of greater value than the sacrificial Rook. Now 2 h8+ is successful, for it forcibly tears away Black’s King from the defense of his Queen. After 2 ... xh8; 3 xg6 White has an easy win.

176B. Black moves. If 1 ... xe7, the Queen’s guard is removed, allowing 2 xd4. Therefore Black must play 1 ... d8 or 1 ... b8. The problem is still “Delenda est Carthago!” – remove the guard! We accomplish this with another check (priority of check!) by playing 2 xc6+. Now Black’s defense topples. White will play 3 xd4.
177B. White moves. He has knocked out the props from under the Knight and can now repeat the process by 2 xb3. After 2 ... xb3, White removes the defenseless Bishop by 3 xd4.
White’s method of winning the Bishop is best described as “removing the guard of the guard.”

178A. Black moves. He sees that the weak link in his opponent’s game is the Bishop. This piece is guarded only by means of other pieces. Black removes the guard by 1 ... xc3, forcing 2 bxc3. White’s defense is about to collapse.

178B. Black moves. He has knocked out one guard. The Pawn push 2 ... g5 disposes of the remaining guard. White has the sad choice of moving the Knight and losing the Bishop, or of saving the Bishop and losing the Knight.
179A. White moves. He is a piece down, but can regain it with 1 xe4+, xe4; 2 e5+ etc. But he wants something more forceful. White works out a daring idea by removing the guard: 1 xc5!!, xf3.
179B. White moves. He must justify his Queen sacrifice. He continues his plan: 2 e1+. This forces 2 ... e7 (interposing the Queen is useless). Now comes 3 xe7+, f8; 4 d8 mate.

title: QUIZ ON REMOVING THE GUARD
texts: 180. White moves. His Queen, now unprotected, attacks Black’s Queen, which is protected. Has White time to remove the guard? How?
181. White moves. Instead of retreating his menaced Knight, he finds a way to remove the guard from the Black Rook which he attacks. How?
182. Black moves. How does he win the Queen by removing its guard?
183. Black moves. How does he win the Queen by removing its guard?

IN CHESS, we must always strive to give our pieces freedom of action. A piece that is not free to go to other squares has no mobility – no freedom of action – and is often in danger of being lost. An attack on it is frequently successful, for the trapped piece has lost the option of fleeing: it has no retreat. In its paralyzed state, it is helpless against the well aimed thrusts of hostile pieces.

One reason why we are constantly admonished to “centralize” pieces is that pieces occupying the center have much more scope for action than have pieces posted at the side of the board. This is particularly true of the Knight.

Yet centralization must not be an automatic process. A piece in the very center of the board whose activity is hampered by its fellowpieces, is exposed to the threat of attack and capture. As for pieces at the side of the board, their mortality rate is frightful!

title: 184. Black moves. He has an easy victim in White’s Knight at the side of the board. This piece has no retreat. But how should the Knight’s awkward situation be exploited? Should Black attack it with his Queen by 1 ... e8? No, for after 2 g3 the Knight would be protected.
texts: The right way is the Pawn stab 1 ... g5! winning the Knight. Against a Pawn’s attack on a piece, neither exchange nor protection can be satisfactory.

title: 185. White moves. His Knight at e3 is attacked. He can move it safely to d1 or c2. But suppose he becomes thoughtlessly aggressive, and wants to post the Knight at d5? The Knight would then have no flight-square – no retreat. Black would play 1 ... c6 winning the Knight.
texts: These two examples illustrate the power of the “weak” Pawn in this type of attack. Flight, when possible, is generally the only defense to a Pawn’s attack.

title: 186. Black moves. He is immediately struck by the fact that White’s Bishop has no retreat. It cannot go forward, while flight is blocked by its own pieces. A Pawn attack will be painful: 1 ... f5 wins the Bishop at once. Such situations often turn up in practical play.

187. Black moves. What feature, above all, stands out in this position? White’s Queen does not have a single move! The Queen, having no retreat, is an easy prey to attack. Black hits out at the paralyzed Queen with the immediately decisive 1 ... h4! White resigns!

188. Black moves. The hostile Queen has no retreat. To win the Queen, it is sufficient to attack it with any piece of lesser value. This hint yields us 1 ... g6, winning the Queen. After 2 xd8+, xd8, White has no relief.
texts: 189. White moves. The candidate for destruction is Black’s Queen, which has an off-side position with few flight squares, while White’s minor pieces have great freedom of action. 1 h4 does the trick, leaving the Queen 14 untouchable squares!

title: 190. White moves. A Knight has least mobility at the side of the board. Black’s Knight has only one flight square: g1. The logical course is therefore 1 f1. White follows this up with 2 g2, winning the Knight, which has no retreat.

191. Black moves. This position is an example of one of the most common no retreat patterns: Black’s Bishop goes Pawn-snatching and soon finds itself in a cul-de-sac. He plays 1 ... xa2? But with 2 b3 the steel trap closes on the Bishop, which has no retreat.

192. Black moves. He plays 1 ... xa2? under the impression that his attack on the Knight will give him the needed time to retreat the Queen to safety. But 2 c4 closes the exit gate. Black’s Queen has no retreat and will be won by 3 a1.

193. Black moves. His Knights are menaced by the threat of f5. If 1 ... c5; 2 f5!, xe5; 3 d4 forking the Knights. Or 1 ... c7; 2 f5!, xe5; 3 d4 and there is no retreat for the Knight of the Rueful Countenance.
texts: 194A. Black moves. His f-Pawn requires protection. Instead of resorting to passive defense, he prefers to counterattack. This takes the form of exploiting the awkward position of White’s Bishop and his Knight on g4. When fleeing from attack, they are bound to get in each other’s way:

195A. White moves. Tarrasch has said: “No piece can be so easily won by Pawns as a Bishop.” The target here is Black’s Bishop at g6. White intends to surround it with Pawns. He begins with 1 xd6+, xd6 (if 1 ... cxd6; 2 f5 with double attack). The sequel is easy.

196A. Black moves. This position from the Ruy Lopez is so old that it is known as the “Noah’s Ark” Trap. As in 195A, the hemming-in process is used to trap a Bishop. Knowing what to look for, Black begins with a forcible move, a capture: 1 ... xd4; 2 xd4. Now another forcible move, a threat: 2 ... c5 attacking White’s Queen.

194B. White moves. The menaced Knight must retreat, and he has only one square for the purpose: h2. But by going there (3 h2), he robs the Bishop of its only flight square. Now 3 ... h4 strikes at the helpless Bishop, which has no retreat and is therefore lost. This is an elaboration of the much simpler position in Diagram 186, where the Bishop obviously had no retreat. Here his flight is prevented.

195B. White moves. He executes his plan with 2 f5 forcing 2 ... h5. Now 3 g4 wins the Bishop, which is attacked and has no retreat. Trapping a Bishop inside a web of Pawns is a fairly frequently seen stratagem. It has some similarity to the method used in Diagram 191.
196B. White moves. Now he sees the coming threat to his Bishop, but he has no choice: he must save his Queen. Once the Queen retreats, 3 ... c4 closes in on the Bishop, leaving it no retreat.
Aside from its practical value, this trap teaches the importance of preparatory forcing moves.
197A. Black moves. He goes after a stray Pawn at the side of the board: 1 ... c2+? After 2 d3 (moving in for the kill), Black is forced to do what he wants to do: 2 ... xa3.
197B. White moves. He is well satisfied with the position: the Black Knight has no moves – no retreat! White swoops down with 3 b3, attacking and winning the miserable Knight.

198A. Black moves. He goes in for a tempting but unsound combination. Relying on a “clever” Knight fork, he wins a Pawn: 1 ... xf5?; 2 xd8, d4+; 3 d3, xb5. Thus Black has regained the sacrificed piece and is a Pawn to the good. It is a case of “ ‘Will you come into my parlor?’ said the spider.”
198B. White moves. His opponent has won a Pawn, but the Knight is stranded on a square where it has little mobility. Again we have the drama of no retreat:
The Knight is lost!

title: QUIZ ON “NO RETREAT”
texts: 199. White moves. One of Black’s pieces has no mobility. Which Pawn move by White will win this piece?
200. White moves. What moves must you make to (a) cut off the retreat of Black’s Bishop and (b) win the Bishop?
201. White moves. Black’s pieces stand in each other’s way. How does White win a piece?

title: 202. White moves. Black’s queen has no mobility – no retreat. What move wins the Queen?
texts: THE SKEWER is a piercing attack which menaces two hostile pieces placed on the same line. As the piece directly attacked moves away, the piece behind it is transfixed on the skewer.

B. H. Wood, who credits the invention of this term to Edgar Pennell, contrasts the skewer with another common kitchen utensil: “Just as a fork is something with more than one prong which can stick into two lumps of meat on your plate at the same time, so the skewer is something that pushes right through a lump of meat, and out the other side.”

A penetrating, “follow-through” attack, the skewer has an effectiveness which is queerly pleasurable. We get a taste of it as children when we set up a row of toy soldiers a little distance apart from each other, and then give the one in front a push. He falls backwards, giving the same motion to the one behind him. He does the same to the soldier behind him, until they have all fallen down. How odd it seems that a slight touch can “follow through” to knock over the last soldier in the line! So it is with the skewer.

To sum up: the skewer attack operates by piercing through a piece in order to transfix another on the same straight line. It is the second piece which is therefore the real target. Opportunities to bring about the skewer may present themselves whenever two enemy pieces are in line on the same file, rank or diagonal.

title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE SKEWER
texts: 203A. Black moves. He sees an opportunity for a skewer attack in the diagonal placement of White’s Bishop on c4 and his Rook at a2. The two pieces are in line, and there ought to be a way ...
1 ... e6 is pointless, as 2 xe6 can be played. What we need is the substitution of White’s Queen for the Bishop at c4. It is very easily arranged: 1 ... xc4; 2 xc4, e6. This is the desired position.

203B. White moves. He is trapped in a classic example of the skewer attack. The previous exchange placed two of White’s major pieces in line on the same diagonal. Major pieces always make good targets, as they can rarely afford capture when menaced by minor pieces. White must discreetly withdraw the Queen; after 3 e2, xa2; 4 xa2 etc. he has lost the exchange without any compensation.

204A. Black moves. He can create a skewer attack by forcing the substitution of White’s King for White’s Bishop. In that case, White will be susceptible to a powerful check by Black’s Bishop. Now for the mechanics: we start with a forcing move, therefore 1 ... xf3+. White must recapture: 2 xf3.
205A. White moves. He pins the Black Bishop, and he can strengthen the pin with 1 c3 or 1 f2. But then comes 1 ... b1+; 2 e1, f2 and Black’s pin wins!
Considering every possible capture or check, White hits on the right idea: a skewer attack!

206A. Black moves. His opponent’s King and Queen are in line on the diagonal. Is a skewer attack possible? Apparently not, as White’s Bishop guards the critical diagonal. But if we can drive the Bishop off, then the skewer will be possible. Therefore: 1 ... f5. The White Bishop cannot be protected, so White plays 2 h4.

204B. Black moves. He has brought about a position where two major enemy pieces occupy the same diagonal – an ideal target for the skewer. Black plays 2 ... g4+. After White moves his King away, 3 ... xd1 leaves Black a piece ahead. The Rook was the real target of Black’s combination.

205B. White plays. By sheer force, he has produced a position ripe for the skewer. Black’s King and Rook are in line on the diagonal. White strikes at both pieces with 2 f2+. After Black’s King moves, White captures the Rook with a piece ahead. Again the Rook was the target.

206B. Black moves. The hindrance to the skewer has been driven off, so that 2 ... h6+ is now possible. This attacks not only the King, but White’s Queen as well. White must play 3 f4, allowing 3 ... exf4+ with complete collapse. (White’s Queen will now be lost just the same. How?)

207A. White moves. If he can force Black’s King back to the first rank, the Rook at h8 will become the real target for a skewer attack. Forcing moves are usually checks or captures: White begins with 1 b7+, d8.
Now Black has King and Rook in line, making a skewer attack feasible. But there is a difficulty!

208A. Black moves. He is so far behind in material (Rook for Queen) that only a miracle can save him. The miracle is available, for the White King and Queen are in line, making possible a skewer in veiled form. At the moment 1 ... b1+ is meaningless, as White’s Bishop on b5 stops the skewer. The Bishop must be removed: 1 ... c6+!

209A. White moves. He has two possible captures: 1 xg2 (which wins) or 1 xf7 (which loses). Like Portia’s suitors, he makes the wrong choice: 1 xf7. The move looks attractive, for it threatens mate and leaves Black with (apparently) nothing but a desperate check or two. But Black heads straight for a skewer! – 1 ... h1+; 2 g3, xh3+; 3 f4.

207B. White moves. He would like to play 2 b8+ (the skewer!) but is prevented by Black’s Knight. He studies the position some more. His Rooks are doubled on the file, so why fear the Knight capture? White continues the planned attack: 2 b8+!, xb8; 3 xb8+, e7; 4 xh8. The skewer has impaled Black’s Rook after all!

208B. White moves. As his King and Queen are menaced by the Knight fork, he must reply 2 xc6. But with the Bishop off the b-file, the skewer is now feasible: 2 ... b1+. White must get his King out of check, losing the Queen and the game.
The combination of fork and skewer is quite artistic.

209B. Black moves. He has driven White’s King to the f-file, so that both their majesties are in line. With the chief actors in their proper places, we are ready for the skewer: 3 ... f3+. White’s King must step aside, letting the skewer penetrate to his Queen (4 ... xf7).
This example and 208B show the value of the skewer for counterattack.

210A. Black moves. He threatens mate at g2, but this is prevented by White’s Queen. But at c2 the Queen is undefended, which gives Black the idea of trying to work out a skewer attack. He needs forcing moves for this, and he has them: plenty of checks.

211A. Black moves. As we know, the favorable elements for a skewer attack are in evidence. White’s Queen is unguarded; his King can be forced back to the second rank, where it will be in line with the White Queen. Play proceeds logically:

212A. White moves. We look for forcing moves, noting that Black has only a limited number of King moves in reply. In such situations the defender is generally helpless to change the inexorable course of events, and he is frequently forced into a skewer position. We begin with 1 d7+, h6 (other King moves allow a mate in one); 2 g7+, h5.

210B. Black moves. He has brought about the desired position by means of two checks. Now comes the skewer with 3 ... h2+ (or, if you wish, 3 ... g2+ – a matter of taste). After White’s King moves, Black plays 4 ... xc2 and it is all over. This type of skewer attack is quite frequent and deserves careful study. See 211A for a very similar procedure.

211B. Black moves. What now follows is clearly indicated. He has driven White’s King and Queen into the same line. An attack on the King will penetrate and find its mark in the unprotected Queen. Black plays 3 ... h2+; White’s King moves off the rank; Black captures the Queen, winning at once.
In 212A the same idea appears in a more elaborate form.

212B. White moves. He is almost ready now for the skewer, aimed at Black’s Queen. First 3 h7+, forcing 3 ... g4. Now Black’s King and Queen are in line – the maximum objective of a skewer attack. White plays 4 xg6+, and the attack pierces through to win the unfortunate Black Queen, as White ends up with 5 xg1.

title: QUIZ ON THE SKEWER
texts: 213. White moves. Black’s Queen and Bishop are in line on the c-file. How does White win a piece by the skewer attack?
214. White moves. Black’s King and Queen are in line on a rank. How does White win the Queen by the skewer attack?
215. Black moves. White’s Queen and Rook (at f1) are on the same diagonal. How does Black win the exchange by a skewer attack?
216. Black moves. How does he force Black’s King and Queen into the same line, in order to win by the skewer attack?

THE COMPLICATIONS of the middle-game frequently result in the exchange of a great many pieces. The players then reach the end-game stage with too few pieces to try for checkmate. It stands to reason that one side with Rook, Knight and four Pawns can hardly force checkmate against an opponent who has Rook, Knight and three Pawns.

How, then, do you win an end-game? There is generally only one way to win an ending. That way is to create an advantage in material so great that further resistance on your adversary’s part becomes absurd.

How can you achieve this objective? By advancing a Pawn to the eighth rank, where it can be promoted to a Queen. This piece is the mating force par excellence, so that if you are a Queen ahead, the method of forcing a win presents no problem. The Queen either (a) carries through a direct mating attack; or (b) captures all your opponent’s remaining pieces and Pawns.

How can one of your Pawns become a fit candidate for promotion to a Queen? It must be converted into a Passed Pawn – it must have no enemy Pawns disputing its forward march on the same file, or on either of the adjacent files; and it must not be blocked by one of its own Pawns.

How do you exploit the advantage of a Passed Pawn? To make the Passed Pawn a fit candidate for queening, you must push the Passed Pawn at every available opportunity. Every step forward by the Passed Pawn brings it that much nearer to its goal (the eighth rank), and creates more and more critical problems for the enemy. As the Pawn approaches the queening-square, your opponent’s attention is necessarily diverted to the problem of blockading your Passed Pawn.
The technique of playing endings (this includes 99% of all endings) can be boiled down to these simple rules:
1 Get a Passed Pawn!
2 Push the Passed Pawn!
3 Clear the way for the Passed Pawn to advance.
4 Capture, exchange or drive off any blockader of the Passed Pawn.
5 When the Passed Pawn has a clear road to the queening-square, simplify by exchanging all the pieces on the board, sacrificing material if necessary.
Observing these rules does not mean that you are to abandon all other tactics and strategy. It does mean that you must push the Passed Pawn every time there is an opportunity to do so.

You must avoid advancing the Passed Pawn recklessly. Your opponent will attempt to interrupt its progress by placing a piece (blockader) in its path. Or he will threaten the Passed Pawn with capture in the event that it marches forward.

Your problem will then be how to get rid of the blockader; or how to control the squares leading to the queening-square; or possibly how to exchange the remaining pieces of both sides, so that the lone survivor, the Passed Pawn, can march in triumph to its coronation.

title: BASIC PATTERN FOR QUEENING COMBINATIONS
texts: 217A. White moves. Follow ing the basic rule for the handling of Passed Pawns, he plays 1 c7. Passed Pawns must be pushed! White threatens to advance the Pawn now to the queening-square. The only way Black can prevent this is to give up his Queen for the Pawn. Whichever course he takes, White remains a whole Rook ahead, with (of course) an easy win.
How did all this come about? Was it luck, or an application of end-game principles?
Diagram 217B shows the position a few moves earlier. Let us see how White (the great master Capablanca) evolved his winning plan.
217B. White moves. His Passed Pawn does not look very formidable.

The Black Queen and Rook halfsurround it. But that in itself is an important point! One “mere” Pawn keeps two such powerful pieces as Black’s Queen and Rook occupied in preventing its further advance.

How does White remove the blockading Black Queen? Not by waiting for the Queen to go away, nor by wishful thinking. The Queen must be forced to move. Once more we search for a violent move: a capture or a check. White plays 1 e5+. Black replies 1 ... g8. (other moves do not affect the outcome). Now White plays another violent move, this time a capture: 2 xd6! Black recaptures: 2 ... xd6, giving the position of 217A. The Pawn is free, the road is clear, the win easy.

218A. White moves. He has a Passed Pawn on the d-file. His course is clear: advance the Pawn! Hence 1 d6, threatening 2 d7. Black dare not defend with 1 ... d3, for then 2 xd3, xd3; 3 d7 and the Passed Pawn becomes a Queen. Therefore Black blockades the Passed Pawn with 1 ... d7. White promptly attacks the blockader with 2 c6.

219A. White moves. He has a Passed Pawn on f6, but apparently there is no way to advance it. Black’s Queen blockades its advance; the Black Bishop exerts pressure on the next square of the Pawn’s march; Black’s Rook guards the last rank. But White applies the magic formula: Remove the blockader!

220A. White moves. He has many winning lines, but the great Paul Morphy, famous for the elegance of his attacking play, naturally seeks the quickest way. His e-Pawn is already advanced to the seventh rank. What stops its promotion? The Black Queen. Therefore that piece must be removed, and here is how it is done: 1 e6+!, xe6 (forced); 2 dxe6.

218B. Black moves. Alas, his blockader (the Knight at d7) must leave his post: 2 ... b8, attacking the Bishop. White replies 3 e8, controlling the next square in the Pawn’s path. Thus all further blockade is impossible. After 4 d7, Black will have to give up his Knight for the Pawn to prevent it from queening. The extra piece will win easily.

219B. White moves. The two obstacles to the Passed Pawn’s advance have been thrust aside, and the Pawn (which should have been kept “under lock and key”) advances: 2 f7! Passed Pawns must be pushed! Black is helpless against the specter of the Pawn’s promotion. There followed: 2 ... d8; 3 f8()+, xf8; 4 xf8+ winning the Queen.

220B. Black moves. He finds himself in an exquisitely painful situation. The Passed Pawn threatens to become a Queen, and Black is powerless to do anything about it! His Rook can do nothing, his King cannot go to f7.
White knew that the Pawn had to be pushed; he knew that the obstacle had to be removed. This amusing tableau is the consequence.

221A. Black moves. He is confronted with the imminent queening of White’s Passed Pawn. As the queening-square is covered by White’s Bishop, the promotion of the Passed Pawn will cost Black his Rook. He therefore plays 1 ... xa4, intending to answer the obvious 2 bxa4 with ... e8 – after which the worst will have been avoided.

222A. Black moves. He wants to push his Passed Pawn to f2 and f1, acquiring a Queen. But White’s Bishop at c5 prevents the advance of the Passed Pawn. 1 ... f4 looks like a good try, but then 2 f2 stops the Passed Pawn. We must proceed according to the slogan Remove the blockader! The right way is 1 ... c4+. White plays 2 d2 edging nearer to the dangerous Passed Pawn.

223A. Black moves. There is no Passed Pawn yet. But by means of a startling sacrifice Black will create a Passed Pawn. Then, according to principle, he will advance the Passed Pawn to the queening-square. He begins with 1 ... f4+, forcing 2 c2. Now he creates the Passed Pawn with 2 ... xg2!

221B. White moves. But he does not care to play the obvious recapture! He studies the situation: he has a Passed Pawn, and Passed Pawns must be pushed! What stops the Pawn from queening? The Rook. Therefore the Rook must be removed! White plays 2 d1! (threat: 3 d8+, xd8; 4 exd8()+ and wins). Black tries 2 ... e8 but must lose after 3 d8! pinning.

222B. Black moves. And now, according to plan, he destroys the blockader: 2 ... xc5. After 3 bxc5 comes the point of the sacrifice of the exchange: 3 ... f2. Note that 4 e2, and 4 g1 are both impossible. Hence White has no way to stop the Passed Pawn from advancing to the last rank and becoming a Queen.
In 223A the blockader is removed even more drastically.

223B. White moves. Having no better reply, he accepts the sacrifice by 3 xg2. In return for the piece, Black has a powerful Passed Pawn. He advances it at once: 3 ... h3. No matter how White plays now, he cannot prevent the Passed Pawn from queening! (Prove this.) Another clever Capablanca ending.

224A. Black moves. The imminent promotion of his Passed Pawn on the b-file is prevented by White’s Queen, which acts as “goal-keeper.” To break through the defense, it is necessary for Black to control the queening-square. Hence he plays 1 ... e4+, so that if 2 g1, b1(), he is a whole Queen ahead! White tries 2 f3.

225A. Black moves. He would like to queen his Passed Pawn without loss of time. But see all the difficulties: White’s Knight controls the queening-square; his King threatens to advance toward the precious Pawn and capture it; finally, Black’s Bishop is attacked. But one startling move changes the picture: 1 ... b2!

226A. Black moves. He has a considerable advantage in material, and his Passed Pawn has a clear road ahead of it. But advancing the Passed Pawn is premature, for example 1 ... d2?; 2 g7+, h8 (not 2 ... h6??; 3 g8 mate!); 3 g8+ and Black’s King cannot escape the perpetual check. Relying on the Passed Pawn he plays 1 ... g4+!

224B. Black moves. His Queen is attacked. Instead of moving it away, he observes the maxim Passed Pawns must be pushed! He therefore plays 2 ... b1(), for now White’s Queen is also attacked. If 3 fxe4, xd1+. No matter what White does on his third move, he must remain a Queen behind. Note the immediately decisive effect of controlling the queening-square.

225B. White moves. His hopes have been dashed. His Knight is an overworked piece: if 2 xb2, c1()+. The Bishop is tabu, but he controls the queening-square; so that if 2 e2 (trying to approach the Passed Pawn), c1(); 3 xc1, xc1 and Black’s material advantage gives him an easy win. A Passed Pawn is no longer a “humble” or “lowly” Pawn.

226B. White moves. He has no good continuation. If 2 h2, xg8; 3 xg8, xg8 and White cannot prevent the Passed Pawn from marching on to become a Queen. No better for White is 2 xg4, hxg4+. If White were not in check now, he could play 3 d5 or 3 f5, followed by 4 e3 stopping the Passed Pawn. But priority of check forces White to play a King move, allowing 3 ... d2 etc.

227A. Black moves. He has a deep plan for making use of his Passed Pawn on e3. He begins with 1 ... c7, intensifying the pin on the Knight. 2 f6+ is refuted by 2 ... xf6; 3 xf6, e2 (threatens 4 ... d1+, as in 221B); 4 c1, cd7 and wins. White therefore tries 2 hd1. Momentarily his Knight is adequately guarded.

227B. Black moves. He has two ways of utilizing his Passed Pawn. One is: 2 ... e2, making White’s attacked Rook an overworked piece. If it moves on the file, then the Pawn advances and becomes a Queen; if the Rook moves on the rank, then White’s Knight is lost. The second method is: 2 ... cxd7; 3 xd7, xd7; 4 xd7, e2! and queens.
228A. White moves. In 226 and 227 we have seen the value of simplifying in order to exploit the strength of a Passed Pawn. Here the combination begins with 1 xf6! forcing 1 ... gxf6.
228B. White moves. Now comes more simplification: 2 xg8+, xg8; 3 xg8. If here 3 ... xa6; 4 xh7 and White is a whole Rook ahead. However, on 3 ... xg8; 4 a7 is decisive.

title: QUIZ ON QUEENING COMBINATIONS
texts: 229. White moves. His Passed Pawn is prevented from advancing by Black’s King. How does he drive off the blockader and win the game?
230. Black moves. His Passed Pawn is prevented from advancing to the queening-square by White’s Bishop. How does Black get rid of the Bishop?

231. White moves. He is ahead in material and has several ways of winning. The quickest method is to simplify by sacrificing, so that his Passed Pawn can march on irresistibly. How does White accomplish this?

232. Black moves. This position will be recognized as a “relative” of 224. How can Black clear away most of the pieces in order to reach a simplified position in which his Passed Pawn can advance victoriously?
“CASTLE EARLY and often!” is the way one wit put it, to emphasize the necessity of getting the King into safety as quickly as possible.

Of the two methods of castling, the King-side is preferable in the great majority of cases; but even there, the King is not quite secure. He is hemmed in by his own Pawns, and cannot advance; yet, being posted on the first rank, he cannot retreat! It is therefore logical to conclude that the King is vulnerable to checks by Rook or Queen on the critical first rank.

This leads to a very natural question: why not assure the King’s safety by advancing one of the Pawns in front of him, in order to create an escape (a “loophole”) for His Majesty? In the end-game stage, such an advance of one of the Pawns is usually in order. During the middle-game, however, it is inadvisable to disturb the position of the Pawns in front of the castled King. An alteration in the Pawn position creates weaknesses which allow hostile pieces to occupy threatening posts whence they can no longer be driven away by Pawns.

title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK
texts: 233A. Black is checkmated. Offhand it might seem that he had been a bit careless and overlooked the mate pictured in the diagram. That this is not the case, can be seen from the next diagram, which shows how this position came about. Later on, we shall see that the weakness of the first rank often makes remarkable combinations possible. Sometimes the result is outright mate, as here; other times, exploitation is indirect.

233B. White moves. Spotting the weakness of Black’s first rank, he plays 1 xa8! The sacrifice is decisive, because it removes one of the defenders of Black’s first rank. After 1 ... xa8 Black has only one Rook guarding his d8, while White has two Rooks trained on it. There follows: 2 d8+, xd8; 3 xd8 mate, as in 233A. In such situations, the creation of a “loophole” by (say) ... h6 is advisable.

234A. Black moves. His Queen and a Rook are trained on White’s first rank, which is guarded by a Rook and Bishop. But the Bishop, being pinned, is paralyzed. Therefore the first rank is vulnerable to attack. Black can invade by sacrificing his Queen: 1 ... e1+! forcing 2 xe1.

235A. White moves. It seems difficult if not impossible to penetrate Black’s first rank. Yet it can be done; and if we look for all possible checks and captures, we find the violent move 1 xd7+! Black plays 1 ... xd7 (1 ... b8 avoids mate but leads to frightful loss of material).

236A. White moves. He attacks the h-Pawn twice, and it is defended only once. Not realizing that his Queen is tied to the defense of the first rank, he plays 1 xh5? With this capture, White’s first rank becomes vulnerable. To prove this, Black sacrifices his Queen with 1 ... xh5! As he cannot remain a Rook down, White retakes: 2 xh5.
234B. Black moves. He recaptures with his Rook, and White is checkmated! Of course White’s Bishop must not interpose.
Since a vulnerable first rank implies mating possibilities, it often permits the most fantastic sacrifices of material. See 244A!

235B. White moves. He continues with occupation of the vulnerable rank: 2 e8+. Black must interpose by 2 ... d8. Now either White Rook captures the Rook, giving checkmate. The brilliant sacrifice 1 xd7+! was perpetrated in actual play by Paul Keres on World Champion Alekhine.

236B. Black moves. He swoops down the whole length of the open file: 2 ... c1+. White interposes with 3 f1; perhaps he overlooks the long-range effect of Black’s Bishop at a6! Black now follows through with 3 ... xf1 mate. (Had White played 3 d1, he would have delayed the mate for one move.) The Queen sacrifice was startling but logical.

237A. Black moves. He wants to invade White’s first rank via the e-file. The play in 235A tells us what to look for. Searching for forcing moves such as checks or captures, Black decides in favor of 1 ... axd2 White recaptures by 2 xd2. (If 2 xd2, xd2; 3 xd2, e1 mate!)

238A. White moves. His Queen and Rook are doubled on the c-file – one of the surest methods of dominating an open line. Such control enables one to use the file as a “jumping-off place” for forcible entry into the hostile position. The opponent’s first rank is a favorite target for this type of attack. White plays 1 g3 with a double threat.

239A. Black moves. It is not clear how he can work up an attack against White’s first rank. But the process of looking for checks and captures again gives us a priceless hint. We begin with 1 ... f3+, which forces White’s King to g1 in order to keep the Rook guarded. Now White’s first rank is vulnerable. The search for checks and captures yields a delightful sequel: 2 ... xf1+!

237B. Black moves. By sacrificing the exchange, he has rendered White’s first rank vulnerable to invasion. Two of the defenders of White’s e1 are gone, so that Black can play 2 ... e1+!; 3 xe1 (or 3 f2, e3 mate), xe1 mate. Black’s first move was an example of removing the guard.

238B. Black moves. His Knight is attacked; hence 1 ... g6, parrying the threat. But White had another threat, made possible by the retreat of the Bishop. This menace, far from obvious, now becomes reality: 2 c8+, xc8; 3 xc8 mate! Black could have avoided this mate, but only at the cost of leaving his attacked Knight in the lurch.

239B. White moves. He has only one reply, 3 xf1, which is resoundingly answered by 3 ... d1 mate. Black’s Pawn at f3 acts as a powerful wedge (actually doing the work of a Bishop or Queen) in blocking the escape of the White King. All of Black’s moves were violent: the more stringently the defense is limited, the easier it is to foresee the consequences.

240A. White moves. He begins with 1 c4+ (1 b3+ has the same effect), which is as strong as it is obvious. Strong because it drives Black’s King into the corner, which makes his first rank vulnerable; obvious because all checks and captures are obvious – they must be the first moves one looks at. Black is forced (why?) to play 1 ... h8. Now comes the brilliant 2 f7!

241A. White moves. He plans to drive Black’s King into the corner. As in 240A, Black’s King will have no mobility – no space to move freely if checked. Knowing what to look for, White plays the brilliant 1 xg7+! Black replies 1 ... xg7 (1 ... h8 allows mate in two – how?). The play continues 2 f7+, h8.

242A. White moves. He plays the “brilliant” move 1 xf6?, reckoning on 1 ... gxf6; 2 xf6+ and mate next move. But, by removing his Rook from the first rank, White has weakened that line. Black reasons that if the other Rook disappears, the vulnerable first rank will be open to mating threats. This leads to the forcing 1 ... xa1!

240B. Black moves. There is no adequate defense to the threat of 3 xg7 mate. If Black plays 3 ... xf7; 4 xe8+ forcing mate next move on the vital rank. 3 ... g8 guards the mate, but 4 xe8 has catastrophic consequences for Black. The chief cause of Black’s downfall is the uselessness of his Queen. Successful attack or efficient defense is difficult without the Queen.

241B. White moves. His brilliant next move should be seen in a flash – look for checks and captures! Black’s first rank, guarded only by a Rook, is attacked by White’s Queen and Rook. How can this concentrated menace be utilized? Answer: 3 f8+! xf8; 4 xf8 mate. Four consecutive checks, two of them captures, led to Black’s downfall.
242B. White moves. Threatened with mate or disastrous loss of material, he is resigned to his fate. He Plays 2 xa1, allowing 2 ... xd1+ and mate in two more moves.
When the Rooks are disconnected, as in 242A, there is often a likelihood that the first rank will be vulnerable to attack.

243A. White moves. He has two attacking “batteries”, the Queen, Bishop and f-Pawn operate against g7; the Rooks control the only open line. To obtain the cooperation of all these forces, he uses a discovered attack: 1 xd7!, xd7; 2 f6! (This Pawn has been unpinned by the sacrifice of the exchange.)

244A. Black moves. He must not snatch at the Queen: 1 ... xb7??; 2 xe8+, xe8; 3 xe8 mate – vulnerable first rank! Instead, Black plays the startling but logical 1 ... xe2! making use of the same weapon to checkmate White! After 2 xe2 White’s first rank is vulnerable. Black proves this immediately as his Rook whizzes down the open file: 2 ... c1+.

245A. White moves. His first observation is that Black’s Rooks are disconnected – always a likely indication of a weak first rank. But White’s goal is not mate; he sees that he can only force the win of a piece. After 1 xb4, xb4; 2 d2 there is a double attack menacing the Rook at b5 and also threatening 3 d8+, xd8; 4 xd8 mate.

243B. Black moves. He is confronted with two threats: 3 xd7 or 3 fxg7+, which wins at least a Rook. To parry both threats, he is forced to play 2 ... fd8. But White wins anyway: 3 xd7! After 3 ... xd7 Black’s first rank is denuded of defenders. He is helpless against the deadly Rook move: 4 e8 mate.

244B. White moves. He cannot stave off mate, but he has a venomous last trap. If he tries 3 e1, then 3 ... xe1+; 4 xe1, xe1 mate. Instead, White plays 3 e1, inviting the blunder 3 ... xe2?? when 4 b8+ (or 4 a8+) forces checkmate on Black! But Black is wary: he plays 3 ... xe1+! 4 xe1, xe1 mate. These witty possibilities deserve careful study.

245B. Black moves. He realizes that if he retreats his Rook from attack, he will be mated as shown. So he defends both threats with 2 ... e7. White plays 3 d8+ just the same. He sees that he will win a piece. Black interposes with 3 ... f8 (not 3 ... xd8??; 4 xd8 mate) and now White wins a piece with 4 xf8+, xf8; 5 d8+ (double attack!)

title: QUIZ ON THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK
texts: 246. White moves. What is the quickest way to remove the guardian of Black’s first rank, making the Black King vulnerable to mate next move?
247. White moves. He cannot force mate, but he can make use of the vulnerable first rank idea to queen his Passed Pawn. How? (Hint: see 221B.)
248. White moves. His situation is apparently critical, for if he plays 1 d6 (forced?) there follows 1 ... xe1+; 2 f2, e4+. Yet White can win by exploiting Black’s vulnerable first rank. How?
249. White moves. Black’s Bishop is paralyzed and prevents the Rook from guarding the first rank. How can White win material by taking advantage of the weakness of Black’s first rank?

WE HAVE SEEN how a piece which is attacked may be won, by making life miserable for its defender. The protector is either destroyed, removed by exchange, or driven off. In all such cases, the defensive function comes to an end.

When these methods of gentle persuasion fail, another effective device is still available. This is to interpose a piece (or force the enemy to do so!) which interferes with the flow of force leading from the piece under attack to its protector. The life-giving current is shut off; the threatened piece is stranded and left to its fate.

Pieces which do not have effective contact with their own forces (such as a Knight stranded at the edge of the board) are particularly susceptible to a break in communications. In general, beware of time-wasting captures which require a piece to travel far afield.

title: BASIC PATTERN FOR BREAKING COMMUNICATION
texts: 250A. Black moves. His powerful pressure against the h-Pawn is neutralized by White’s Queen. Black breaks the line of communication by 1 ... d3!!
250B. White moves. If he plays 2 xd3, Black continues 2 ... xh3+; 3 g1, g2 mate. Or if 2 xd3, xd3; 3 xd3, d6+ (double attack!) and wins.

251A. Black moves. His Bishop attacks White’s Knight, which is protected by his Rook. The Rook cannot be driven off, nor threatened with capture or exchange. Yet its protective power can be nullified by 1 ... d2+, forcing 2 c1.

251B. Black moves. He still attacks the Knight, but it is no longer guarded by the Rook. The line of communication has been snapped by the forced retreat of White’s King. Consequently Black wins easily by simply removing the Knight: 2 ... xe1.

252A. Black moves. He plays to win a Pawn, without realizing that he will be breaking the line of communication that guards a vital piece. He captures by 1 ... gxf4 and after 2 gxf4, he snatches the seemingly undefended Pawn by 2 ... xf4?

252B. White moves. His Queen attacks Black’s Queen, which is protected by a Rook. He severs the line of communication with 3 g3+. If now 3 ... f7, Black’s Queen has lost the protection of the Rook, so that 4 xf4+ wins at once.

253A. White moves. He pins and doubly attacks Black’s Bishop at e7, which is doubly defended. To drive away Black’s Queen from the defense, White plays 1 f4. Now Black cannot play 1 ... xf4?? (removal of the guard) because of 2 xe7 mate. Or, if 1 ... f6, the skewer 2 g5 makes the pin decisive. Black therefore tries 1 ... c5.

253B. White moves. He plays 2 d6, striking for the third time at the pinned Bishop, which is overwhelmed, as it is attacked three times and defended only once. The d-Pawn has added its weight to the attack; but more important is the fact that it has wedged itself between Bishop and Queen, cutting their line of communication. Black is lost; if 2 ... cxd6; 3 xe7 mate.

254A. Black moves. He can win a piece, but how? His Rook at b2 attacks the Bishop, which, however, is defended. How can Black break the line of communication when there is no line of communication?! The answer is: by creating such a line! Thus: 1 ... d5. White replies 2 e8, for if 2 c4, b5 wins a piece by double attack! (Retreat by the Bishop to d3 or e2 was of course impossible.)
Black has separated the Queen and Bishop, yet the Queen still exercises protection from a4 to e8.

254B. Black moves. With the venomous Pawn push 2 ... b5, he breaks the line of communication, attacking the Queen and winning the Bishop. Creating a line of communication in order to break it is a novel device! There is an analogy in the story of the preacher who was exhorting his congregation to repent, and save themselves from the lot of sinners in the Hereafter – where “There will be weeping and wailing and gnashing of teeth.” “Suppose I have no teeth?” an old lady asked. “Teeth will be provided,” was the preacher’s quick reply.
ON THE CHESSBOARD, surprise is nothing more than logic that packs a wallop. The impact of surprise thrills the perpetrator, pleases the kibitzer, crushes the victim.
Many years ago, the distinction was subtly established by the famous lexicographer who was caught (by his wife, of course) in the act of kissing the maid.
“Why, John!” his wife exclaimed, “I’m surprised!”
Even in this trying situation (which might be described as the basic pattern for the surprise move), the dictionary-compiler’s training did not desert him.
“You’re not surprised,” he answered. “I’m surprised. You’re astonished.”
Chess is so prolific in the variety of combinations it produces that it may seem pointless to isolate a certain kind of move and call it a “surprise” move.

We have already been taught to “expect the unexpected.” No matter how brilliant a move may be, it cannot startle us if it is also the logical move – the move that conforms to the pattern of the combination we are seeking.

Yet there are times when a move is so wildly fantastic that it jolts us out of our seats – until we realize that for all its bizarre appearance, it is earnestly sane and carefully evaluated. Such a move, which ruthlessly rips away the superficial aspects of the position, may rightfully be called a “surprise” move.

For the audience witnessing a game between experts, a surprise move has the thrill an unexpected knockout gives to fight fans watching two evenly matched prize fighters. For the reader of master games, a surprise move gives more joy than seven miles of painfully correct analysis. The surprise move has all the delicious quality of a witty remark lighting up a learned discourse.

When do such moves occur? Usually at the beginning of a combination: a piece is given up to smash the hostile King’s position by a mating attack. But often the surprise move can be played with incomparably greater effect as the last in a series of innocuous moves or exchanges, in a position which seems completely harmless.
This second course is a great favorite with the modern master, who finds it highly effective, because less hackneyed, to wind up his combination with a stinging surprise.

It may seem out of place to give advice on how to guard against surprise moves, when the greatest masters have at one time or another succumbed to their electrifying effect. But the habit of examining every possible check or capture will reduce your losses.

The positions which follow may be studied with profit, but their chief purpose is to delight the reader with their fireworks effects. As for the victims of surprise moves, they may agree with Caesar, who, when asked which sort of death was the best, said: “That which is unexpected.”

255A. Black moves. He invades enemy territory by 1 ... e2, threatening 2 ... xf2 mate or 2 ... xf2 mate. It is relatively best for White to make a temporary escape with 2 h3, with a prosaic loss in prospect. But he instinctively guards the weak spot with 2 f1?

256A. White moves. He has given up a piece for a strong attack, which is all the more virulent because Black’s Queen is cut off from the defense. For his concluding combination, he has prepared a charming sacrifice. He plays 1 g7+ forcing 1 ... f7. And now the sur prise: 2 e6+!!

257A. White moves. How can his Queen participate in the attack with no loss of time? To avoid giving Black a breathing spell, White plays 1 b5! Black must do something about his Queen – at once! Therefore he has no time to attend to his King’s welfare. Black replies 1 ... xb5 (other Queen moves allow the same continuation).

255B. Black moves. He has a surprise move: 2 ... xf3! White captures by 3 gxf3, whereupon Black gracefully winds up the White King’s career with 3 ... g6 mate – an “epaulet” mate! The White Rooks which hover so anxiously around their King actually bring about his downfall!

256B. Black moves. Rocked on his heels by the unexpected Queen sacrifice, he has no choice but to accept: 2 ... xe6. The capture is answered by 3 dxe6 mate! Despite the army of White pieces trained on Black’s King, it remained for the not-so-humble Pawn to deal the death -blow!

257B. White moves. His clever Bishop sacrifice cleared the way for action by the Queen – but not at once (2 h5??, f1 mate!). Again time is of the essence – another violent move is needed: 2 xh7+!, forcing 2 ... xh7. Now White mates by 3 h5+, h6; 4 xh6 mate. “Surprise is nothing more than logic that packs a wallop.”

258A. White moves. Threatened with mate on the move, he hits on the superb surprise move 1 b6+!! Pundits would analyze this fearless plunge into a nest of hostile Pawns as a Knight fork, based on a pin (Black’s c-Pawn is paralyzed), plus a sacrifice as a clearance for the White Queen. But for our purposes the Knight move is a magnificent stroke, too delightful to desecrate by dissection!

259A. Black moves. He sees the three-move threat of mate with 1 h7+, f8; 2 e6+, fxe6; 3 xg7 mate. What more natural than 1 ... xd4 parrying the threat and winning a piece? But Black gets a rude awakening, as White replies with the electrifying 2 h8+.
260A. Black moves. He plays 1 ... e3. This attacks the Queen. If 2 xe3?? xg2 mate. If White retreats his Queen from attack, then 2 ... xg3; 3 xg3, xg3 with a piece ahead.
But White thinks he sees a way out: gaining time with a check, he will remove one of the Rooks and then pin the dangerous Queen: 2 xg6+, fxg6; 3 c4.

258B. Black moves. He captures: 1 ... axb6. Utilizing the open a- file, White replies 2 a8 mate. (Black could have avoided the mate by moving his King in reply to 1 b6+!! – but this would have meant losing the Queen.)
This is a perfect example of the value of studying every possible check or capture.

259B. Black moves. He has no choice: he must play 2 ... xh8, allowing 3 xh8 mate. The Queen sacrifice seems a lot less startling to one who is familiar with mating patterns (see the section on that subject). An early combination by Dr. Euwe, who later became World Champion.

260B. Black moves. Apparently White has defended with genuine skill. He has avoided the loss of a piece, and he is about to exchange Queens. True, Black can now win by 3 ... xc4; 4 xc4, d3 and 5 ... d1. But at least White will be losing creditably.
Instead, Black mates on the move: 3 ... xh3 mate! The pinned Queen is still pinning!

261A. White moves. He is the exchange ahead – enough to win, but there is no obvious immediate decision. However, White has a beautiful surprise move which gives Black his quietus: 1 d5!!, offering his Rook in four different ways! Despite these alternative ways of capturing, the White Rook is anything but vulnerable.

262A. Black moves. Since White’s King cannot move, mate can be administered by any Black checking piece safe from capture. This is the logical explanation of the extraordinary play that follows: 1 ... xb2!! threatening 2 ... xh2 mate. If now 2 h3, h2 or if 2 h1, e1, forcing mate in either case. White prefers to be “shown.” He plays 2 xb2, which is answered by the stunning 2 ... e5!!
263A. Black moves. He begins with 1 ... xh3! relying on a Knight fork (if 2 gxh3? the family check 2 ... f3+ wins at once). But White has a resource: counterattack with 2 c5.
Black (Marshall) plays 2 ... g3!!! The Queen must be taken, as 3 ... xh2 mate is menaced.

261B. Black moves. Which way does he want to be mated? If 1 xd5; 2 f6 mate (overworked Queen). If 1 ... xd5; 2 f8 mate (vulnerable first rank). Finally, if 1 ... exd5 or 1 ... xd5; 2 xd8 mate (breaking communications)! Nor can Black really refuse the Rook, as 2 xd8 mate and 2 xd4 are threatened.

262B. White moves. Life is still very difficult for him, the threat being 3 ... g6 mate! He has no alternative but to play 3 fxe5. But now the real blow descends, for Black’s earlier sacrifices, brilliant though they were, served only as preliminaries. Black plays 3 ... g5 mate! It was the fatal position of the White King that made the surprise moves logical.

263B. White moves. His opponent has just played the most brilliant move in the history of chess! White is helpless: if 3 hxg3, e2 mate! If 3 fxg3, e2+; 4 h1, xf1 mate. Or 3 xg3, e2+; 4 h1, xg3+; 5 g1, e2+ with a piece ahead. So White resigns. “Some of Marshall’s most sparkling moves look at first like typographical errors” (Napier).

THERE HAS NEVER BEEN a good definition of the word “combination.” We can come close to the real meaning by saying that a combination is a series of forcing moves which result in checkmate, gain of material, or improvement in position. In a combination we impose our will on the opponent by forcing his replies.
The patterns that we have studied so far – the pin, the Knight fork, the double attack, the discovered check and the rest, are all fundamental; they form the basis of combination play.

When we combine two or more of these themes – say a pin followed by a Knight fork – we are on the way to understanding and playing combinations on a grand scale, the kind that mark the play of a master. Combinations which at first sight may seem difficult to understand, become clear and simple when broken down into their component parts. The amazing combinations of Alekhine, Keres, Capablanca and the other great masters can be reduced to basic elements that we know and understand from our study of the preceding chapters.

What these masters create on the chessboard may be compared appropriately to the full stage presentation of the master magician. The layman is bewildered by the overpowering procession of illusions. The magician’s colleagues, on the other hand, see in his performance “nothing more” than a grand combination of familiar themes. The sleight-of-hand, the shuffling and concealment of cards, the palming of coins, the disappearing goldfish, the woman sawed in half – all these are only the equivalent of the chess master’s bag of tricks: the pins, Knight forks, double attacks and discovered checks.

There is one important distinction between the magician and the chess master. When the layman discovers how illusions are created, there is a great psychological let-down. When the chess student is given a rational explanation of the mechanics of chess combination, his enjoyment of the game is intensified.

title: BASIC PATTERN FOR COMBINED OPERATIONS
texts: 264. Black moves. He sees that 1 ... h3+ wins against all four possible replies: if 2 gxh3, xf2+; 3 h1, xh2 mate. If 2 xh3, xe4, and White’s overworked Rook cannot recapture; for if 3 xe4, d1+ leads to mate on the vulnerable first rank. If 2 f1, xf2 mate or 2 ... xf2 mate. Finally, if 2 h1, xf2+ wins the Queen by a Knight fork.

265A. Black moves. He sees an attractive Knight fork which threatens King and Queen: 1 ... e4+. But White has a Pawn guarding the crucial square! The unthinking player would discard the idea at this point; but one familiar with combination patterns looks further ahead. He makes the impossible moves become possible! Black plays 1 ... e4+! forcing 2 fxe4.

266A. White moves. Will it be giving away the plot to say that White wins material by a combination involving a Knight fork followed by a pin? The first link in the chain is an attack on Black’s Queen: 1 g5. (His object, improbable as it may seem, is to play 2 e6, forking the Black Rooks.) Black replies 1 ... e8, hoping to guard the vital square.

267A. White moves. He notes that the mobility of Black’s Queen is severely constricted. How can White exploit this state of affairs? He looks for a violent move. 1 b4, attacking the Queen and unpinning the Knight, answers the purpose. After the forced reply 1 ... b6, White follows up with 2 xd5, this time forcing 2 ... c6.
